This is a tutorial for making a USB 2.0 hub! By the end of this tutorial, you will learn how to source parts, design a PCB, generate production files, and order from fabs!

![](./pxl-20260415-073730258-1-.webp)

## Chapter 0: Preface

<Checkpoint>
  A USB hub is: a device that connect to a computer USB port and provides 4 more USB ports.
</Checkpoint>

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### Chapter 0.2: USB versions

|                     | USB 1.1          | USB 2.0          | USB 3.2            |
| ------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
| Release date        | 1998             | 2000             | 2008               |
| Speed               | 12Mbps (1.5MB/s) | 480Mbps (60MB/s) | 5000Mbps (625MB/s) |
| Cost and difficulty | Very Low         | Low              | High and hard      |

<Warning>
  With USB 1.1 speed, a YouTube video can take around 1-15 minutes to copy from one place to another, while with USB 2.0 speed, it can take 3-30 seconds.
</Warning>

<Checkpoint>
  USB 2.0 is the middle ground between speed and cost for our design.
</Checkpoint>

## Chapter 1: Sourcing parts

### Chapter 1.1: The USB hub IC (the brain of the device)

Common USB hub integrated controllers (ICs):

- WCH CH334 (we will be using this)
- TERMINUS FE1.1S
- CoreChips SL2.1A

Why do we use the CH334?:

|                  | CH334                                                 | Fe1.1s                                                          | SL2.1A                                                  |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cost             | $0.57                                                 | $0.69                                                           | $0.26                                                   |
| Complexity       | Low (integrated crystal, only one external capacitor) | High (requires external precise resistor, crystal, capacitors)  | Low (integrated crystal, only three external capacitor) |
| Transaction Mode | MTT                                                   | STT                                                             | STT                                                     |

<Checkpoint>
  What is transaction mode?

  - Transaction mode is how a USB hub ic was designed. STT stands for Single Transaction Translator and MTT stands for Multiple Transaction Translator.
  - Imagine STT being a road with one lane, and MTT being a road with multiple lane. While your camera is busy transmitting data over one lane, with STT your other devices would be laggy, but with MTT it will not. Imagine your mouse lagging or your keyboard delaying keystrokes while your camera feed is also getting interference from other devices
    <ReadMore>
      <ExternalGuide
        href="https://superuser.com/a/1847637"
        title="What is the difference between the STT and MTT in USB 2.0 interface?"
      />
    </ReadMore>
</Checkpoint>

### Chapter 1.2: USB hub IC external components

External components like capacitors, crystals, inductors, etc. are often accompanied with the IC to ensure the power rails have enough decoupling to prevent high frequency noise to affect its operation.

To find out what is needed, let's investigate the datasheet!

<Step title="Finding and downloading the IC datasheet">
  We are using the CH334 from WCH, so let's search that up in Google.

  ![](data:image/png;base64,)The first result links us directly to the IC manufacturer website for the datasheet.

  Going through the link, we can download the datasheet:

  ![](data:image/png;base64,)

  <Step title="Reading the datasheet" />
</Step>

The datasheet is where you will find most of the information about the IC provided by the manufacturer. Values in the datasheet are the most accurate and tested by the manufacturer themselves, as well as their example applications. 

![](data:image/png;base64,)

<Checkpoint>
  Datasheets are your first stop for any information about the parts.
</Checkpoint>

<Step title="Analyzing the application notes">
  Application notes are example wiring schematic from the manufacturer and they usually includes components that is meant to work with the chip. Usually for simpler chip, you can just copy the example schematic, but for more complex chip, reading the electrical characteristics and the ratings section is highly recommended.

  ![](data:image/png;base64,)&#x20;

  An application from the CH334 datasheet. This application includes multiple parts such as connectors, a crystal, several capacitors, and a fuse. We can simplify this further as from my experience, it doesn't need this much components.

  ![](data:image/png;base64,)

  Another application for the CH334. Notice how this one doesn't have a crystal, but it still have connectors and capacitors. Those are your necessary components to build a USB hub.

  CH213K included in the application is a power protection chip. Feel free to add this into your design but it is not necessary.

  C4 will drip overcurrent protection (OCP) on the host device, so we will replace it with one 10uF ceramic capacitor per port.

  C2 can be omitted. Learn more [here](https://www.signalintegrityjournal.com/articles/1589-the-myth-of-three-capacitor-values)

  <Checkpoint>
    You should be able to navigate other parts' datasheet easily now!
  </Checkpoint>
</Step>
